text: When you type a web address into your browser, a quick lookup called DNS resolution turns that human-friendly name into the numeric IP address computers use to find each other. First, the browser checks its own cache to see whether it has looked up the domain recently. If it finds a saved answer there, it uses it right away and skips the rest. If not, the request goes to a recursive resolver, a server usually run by your internet provider or a public DNS service. The resolver works through the naming hierarchy one step at a time. It asks a root server first, and the root points it to the right top-level domain (TLD) server, such as the one for ".com". The TLD server then sends the resolver to the authoritative server for that specific domain, which returns the actual IP address. The resolver passes the answer back to your browser, and both of them cache it for a set time called the time to live (TTL). A typical TTL is 300 seconds, or five minutes. This balances speed and freshness, so repeat visits load quickly while changes to the address still spread soon after they're made.
